extra_misconceptions.fact: A boat in neutral can still have slow propeller rotation or accidental gear engagement, so the engine must be turned off.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Shifting a towboat into neutral completely stops the propeller from spinning near a swimmer at the stern.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Odorless carbon monoxide concentrates directly above the swim platform and water surface, causing rapid unconsciousness.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Open air behind a moving or idling towboat disperses exhaust fast enough to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Vigorous rubbing can damage cold tissue and push cold blood to the core; remove wet gear and apply gradual core warmth instead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing cold extremities vigorously is the fastest way to warm a water skier showing early signs of hypothermia.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Wind and water evaporation mask heavy sweat loss on a boat, requiring regular water intake before thirst develops.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cool lake spray prevents dehydration and heat exhaustion for skiers and observers out in direct summer sun.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to hang onto the boat swim platform while the engine is idling between runs?
Which physical indicator distinguishes heatstroke from heat exhaustion during an all-day session on the lake?
What happens to the tow rope if a fallen skier fails to release the handle immediately upon hitting the water?
Under what condition does the boat driver shut off the engine completely before approaching a downed skier?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Inflatable PFDs are not rated for high-speed water impact and can fail to keep a stunned or unconscious skier afloat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Any Coast Guard approved inflatable belt pack or suspender PFD is suitable for high-speed waterskiing and wakeboarding.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Water Sports Safety Code requires a dedicated safety observer in addition to the driver so the driver watches ahead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wide rear-view mirrors on a ski boat allow an experienced driver to tow a skier legally without a separate observer.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A loose life jacket rides up around the ears and face upon entering the water, obstructing breathing and vision.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Buying a slightly oversized life jacket gives a growing Scout better arm mobility without reducing flotation safety.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Glare and surface ripples hide submerged stumps and sandbars, so towing requires a minimum safe depth of five to six feet.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Underwater hazards are easy to spot from the towboat if the water surface looks calm and clear near the shoreline.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms that a buckled water sports life jacket will not ride up over your chin in deep water?
Why is it dangerous to wear an inflatable life jacket or a loose keyhole vest while wakeboarding or waterskiing?
Where should a Scout position the towboat relative to swimmers, docks, and anchored fishermen under the Safety Code?
Which physical indicator on a foam vest shows that the buoyancy material has degraded and must be retired?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every participant must complete the full 100-yard swimmer test and float before attempting any towed water sports activity.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wearing a Coast Guard approved life jacket during water sports eliminates the need to pass the Scouting swimmer test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The final 25 yards must be swum using an easy, resting backstroke to demonstrate energy conservation in open water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimming all 100 yards with a fast freestyle sprint fulfills the Scouting America swimmer classification test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The first 75 yards require coordinated surface strokes such as crawl, breaststroke, sidestroke, or trudgen with rhythmic breathing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Dog paddling or swimming underwater counts toward the 75-yard strong stroke portion of the swimmer qualification.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The swimmer test requires resting by floating as motionless as possible for one minute with minimal survival movement.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Treading water vigorously with constant arm and leg movement satisfies the one-minute floating requirement.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a tired skier waiting for boat pickup if they cannot transition into an easy resting backstroke?
Which physical indicator during the first 75 yards shows that a swimmer is maintaining a strong, sustainable stroke?
Why is it dangerous to attempt a deepwater ski start before verifying the one-minute resting float requirement?
Under what condition does the swimmer test require a feetfirst entry into water over the Scout's head?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Clasping both hands overhead forms a high-visibility arch that confirms the skier is safe and visible to other boaters.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Waving one arm casually from the water is the standard signal to tell the boat driver that a fallen skier is unhurt.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pointing left or right indicates a turn direction, while patting the top of the head signals returning to the dock.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pointing directly toward the shoreline tells the safety observer and boat driver to take the skier back to the dock.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A thumb pointing up instructs the driver to increase boat speed, whereas the thumb-and-forefinger OK sign means speed is good.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Giving a thumbs-up gesture while being towed tells the observer that the boat speed is comfortable and steady.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The safety observer watches the skier and relays every hand signal verbally so the driver keeps full attention on the water ahead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The boat driver should watch the skier continuously to read hand signals directly without relying on the observer.

extra_socratic_questions: Which hand signal must a fallen skier display immediately in the water so approaching boats can see them clearly?
What happens to crew coordination if the safety observer fails to relay the skier's speed signal to the boat driver?
Where should a Scout position their hand when patting the head to signal returning to the dock after a run?
Why is it dangerous to shout verbal commands toward the towboat instead of using standard visual hand signals?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Bending the arms shifts body weight forward over the ski tips and causes a fall; arms must stay straight while knees stay tucked.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling the tow handle toward the chest with bent elbows helps a skier stand up faster during a deepwater start.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Locked knees transmit wake impact directly to the hips and cause a bounce fall; flexed knees and ankles act as shock absorbers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stiffening the legs while crossing the boat wake provides maximum stability against the turbulent wave crest.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Bending at the waist pushes weight over the front of the skis; edging across the wake requires leaning away from the boat's pull.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaning forward from the waist toward the boat helps generate enough speed to cut outside both wakes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Jumping in wearing skis risks twisting ankles or hitting the boat hull; enter the water first and put the equipment on in deep water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Jumping from the swim platform with skis already strapped on is the safest way to enter the water for a start.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your balance during a deepwater start if you pull the tow handle into your chest by bending your arms?
Where should a Scout position the tow rope relative to two skis or a wakeboard before signaling the driver to tighten line?
Under what condition does flexing your knees absorb the crest impact when cutting across both wakes and back to center?
Why is it dangerous to stand up abruptly before the skis plane on the surface during the initial boat acceleration?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Dry rubber creates high friction against skin and can tear the binding or twist an ankle; always wet both foot and binding first.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Dry rubber ski bindings slide onto a bare foot more easily on shore than bindings that have been dipped in lake water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Overtightened bindings cannot release during high-torque twisting falls, which increases the risk of severe foot and ankle sprains.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cinching wakeboard or ski bindings as tight as possible prevents ankle injuries by keeping the board attached in every crash.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Extending the legs in deep water causes a swimmer to tip backward or sink; tuck the knee to the chest to push the foot straight down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Kicking both legs straight out in deep water makes it easier to push a foot into a floating water ski binding.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cold water shrinks foot volume and lubricates rubber, requiring a final snug adjustment in the water so the ski stays on during start.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Adjusting binding size in deep water is unnecessary if the straps were already set loosely on the boat platform.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your ankle during a hard fall if a ski or wakeboard binding is tightened beyond a snug release fit?
Which physical indicator on shore confirms that a binding holds your heel firmly without cramping your foot arch?
Why is it dangerous to swim after a lost ski before checking for approaching boat traffic and raising your safe signal?
Where should a Scout position the ski tip while floating in deep water to slide a wet foot cleanly into the binding?
